title: George Russell salary: converting hourly pay to annual using Australian standards
description: Learn how to convert George Russell's salary from hourly to annual using Australian pay standards, including tax, super, and the National Minimum Wage.
salarySummary: For a standard full-time role at 38 hours per week, the annual salary is hourly rate × 38 × 52.

faqs.q: What is the National Minimum Wage from July 2026?
faqs.a: From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Casual employees receive $33.05 per hour including the 25% casual loading. These rates are set by the Fair Work Ombudsman and apply to award-free employees.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from my hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then by 52. For a full-time role, we assume 38 hours per week. For example, $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,269.44 per year. This is gross pay before tax and super. Use [the timesheet](/) to do this calculation automatically.

faqs.q: Does super come out of my salary or is it on top?
faqs.a: Superannuation guarantee contributions are paid on top of your salary, not deducted from it. From 1 July 2026, the rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. Your employer must pay this into a super fund separately.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the hourly-to-annual conversion: a look at George Russell's salary and Australian pay standards

When you hear about a high-profile figure like George Russell, you might wonder how their salary compares to everyday Australian pay. While the exact George Russell salary isn't published by the Fair Work Ombudsman or the Australian Taxation Office, the same formula used to convert any hourly rate to an annual figure applies. This article explains that formula, the key assumptions, and how Australian pay standards differ for minimum wage earners, award-covered workers, and high-income earners.

### The basic formula: hourly rate × hours per week × 52

The standard conversion from hourly to annual pay is straightforward: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a full-time employee in Australia, the typical working week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Act. So the formula becomes:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, using the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 of $26.44 per hour:

$26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,269.44 per year (approximately)

This matches the Fair Work Ombudsman's weekly figure of $1,004.90 when multiplied by 52 ($1,004.90 × 52 = $52,254.80, a small rounding difference). The formula assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. It's a baseline estimate.

### Fortnightly pay: a useful intermediate

Many Australian employees are paid fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, simply double the weekly amount. Using the minimum wage example:

Weekly: $1,004.90
Fortnightly: $2,009.80

This can help you budget or compare with salary offers that quote a fortnightly figure. The [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman provide award-specific rates that may include higher minimums, allowances, and penalty rates.

### National Minimum Wage vs award rates vs casual loading

Australia has a multi-tiered pay system. The National Minimum Wage is the legal floor for employees not covered by an award or agreement. From 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour for permanent employees. Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top, making their minimum $33.05 per hour. This loading compensates for the lack of paid leave.

However, most employees are covered by a modern award, which sets higher minimum rates for specific industries and occupations. Award rates vary widely. For example, the Children's Services Award and Pharmacy Award have recently seen increases due to gender-based undervaluation reviews. The Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides list the exact rates for each classification.

If you're a casual worker under an award, you generally receive the award's base rate plus the 25% casual loading. The [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains this in more detail.

### Applying the formula to George Russell's salary

George Russell is a Formula 1 driver, a profession not covered by Australian awards. His actual salary is not publicly available from the Fair Work Ombudsman, the Australian Bureau of Statistics, or the Australian Taxation Office. Media reports suggest figures in the millions, but we cannot verify those. If we were to apply the hourly conversion, we would need to know his hourly rate (if he were paid by the hour) and an assumed number of working hours per week. For a driver, the 'working week is not 38 hours, but for the sake of demonstration, let's assume a hypothetical hourly rate of $500. Using the formula:

$500 × 38 × 52 = $988,000 per year

But this is purely illustrative. For high-income earners, the super guarantee maximum contribution base of $270,830 applies, meaning super is only paid on earnings up to that amount. Tax also changes at higher brackets. The [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page covers these rules.

### Tax and super considerations

The annual gross figure from the formula is before tax and super. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low-income earners). For a minimum wage earner, the tax would be minimal. For a high earner like George Russell, the top marginal rate applies.

Superannuation guarantee is 12% of ordinary earnings, paid by the employer on top of the salary. It is not deducted from the employee's pay. The maximum contribution base is $270,830, so for earnings above that, no additional super is required.

### Using the timesheet and pay guides

To calculate your own annual salary from an hourly rate, use [the timesheet](/). Simply enter your base hourly rate and check the casual loading box if applicable. The tool will show your weekly, fortnightly, monthly, and annual gross pay, along with estimated tax and super. For award-specific rates, refer to the [pay guides](/blog) on the Fair Work Ombudsman website.

### Conclusion

The hourly-to-annual conversion is a simple multiplication, but the assumptions you make matter. For most Australian employees, the standard 38-hour week is a safe starting point. For someone like George Russell, without official data, we can only demonstrate the method. Whether you're earning the minimum wage or a seven-figure salary, the formula remains the same: hourly rate × hours per week × 52. Use the tools and guides available to get an accurate picture of your own pay.
